doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

chapter: Rock and roll and the decline of jazz work
title: Bebop, Dixieland and doo wop: changing tastes and the money
summary: Musical controversies, his fascination with bebop, and how young listeners' disposable income shifted work to doo wop.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: That’s very interesting. I wanted to ask you something you briefly touched on before. You were talking about rock & roll. You know musical styles and what’s popular changes a lot but do you remember specifically what it felt like for jazz-based musicians around here when rock & roll started to take over?
Well you know we’ve always had controversies with the musicians. The moldy figs against the beboppers. What did Louis say?

So there is always a controversy. I mean even if you read history in New Orleans, how there seemed to be controversies. You have the different schools. As I guess each age has its musical culture, musical taste, their fad, or whatever you want to call it. So I’m speaking for myself. I came up in the big band era. Then when bebop came in I was just fascinated with it, just absolutely fascinated with it. The improvisation, the tempos, the soloists, the independence that the drummers had. It was just fascinating. So then — we tolerated Dixieland, because you know we gave it its due, gave it the credit because it’s improvisation, it’s mainly improvisation. They had their songs and their routines, but then in the meantime the soloists, they improvised. And a guy like Sidney Bechet was way ahead of himself. Who knows? Bird might of taken from Bechet because he was a bad cat. Okay so you respect that. You listen to it. But then the doo wop came in. All these singing groups. Well the kids, the young kids, with disposable income, suddenly there was all of this money because the veterans, the veterans then and the war workers but mainly veterans, they were going to school, they were buying homes, raising families, and suddenly this surplus income, the money started to get tight. And here comes the young kids with their music and suddenly the club owners, you know the business is falling off. So some of them were jumping on the bandwagon. As a matter of fact in the mid-sixties I know when I went to work at the Oakland office they would have concerts, some of these promoters, they would promote a concert on the weekend.
